description: We are four sophomores majoring in Information Systems Engineering who are eager to learn and turn data into useful tools. We have a foundation in programming, databases, and systems analysis; we work well as a team; and we’re not afraid to learn new technologies. We’re interested in satellite data processing because we believe that NASA’s open data can solve real-world problems. We want to build something useful for those who use it.
summary:
Virtual Satellite Unification is a web application that unifies five NASA FIRMS active-fire satellite records (MODIS on Terra and Aqua; VIIRS on S-NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21) into a single coherent time series from 2000 to 2026. Every time a satellite was added, the record showed more fires without necessarily more fire on the ground. Our pipeline corrects that effect: it standardizes and filters detections, collapses them into events by H3 cell and day, and applies a calibration by constellation and month with 95% confidence intervals. An independent audit, which blocks publication on any error, validates the result. In Argentina, 146.3 million raw rows were reduced to 2.67 million events, with 0 FAIL.

Users pick an area of interest and get a fire activity calendar, each year’s anomaly against the historical median, and the harmonized data as CSV. Early-warning services, scientists and land managers can anticipate critical periods, guide monitoring and quickly spot an unusual season. The roadmap adds near-real-time alerts with NOAA-21 and global scaling. It is lightweight, location-agnostic and extends to new countries and satellites without a redesign.
details:
1. What does Gitpush.tito do?

Virtual Satellite Unification is an interactive web application that turns five satellite fire records, until now incomparable with one another, into a single coherent time series from 2000 to 2026. It works for any region of the planet, although due to time constraints it is only implemented for some countries.

The user chooses an area of interest and the application delivers:

-Fire Activity Calendar: when and how intensely it burned in that area, day by day and year by year, in a view that can be understood at a glance.

-Anomaly by Year vs. Median: how much the activity of a period deviates from the historical median of the place, to detect unusual seasons.

-CSV download: the harmonized data, ready to use in your own analyses, reports or alert systems.

In other words: it answers the question “is what is happening right now in this place normal?” with evidence from more than two decades.

2. How does it do it?

The underlying problem is that between 2000 and 2026 the number of satellites grew from 1 to 5 (Terra, Aqua, S-NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21). With more passes and better resolution, more fires are detected, not because there is more fire but because we are looking more often. Comparing those series directly creates artificial jumps. We solve this with a four-stage pipeline, plus a web data store and an independent quality audit. The figures shown come from the real Argentina run (2000-11-01 → 2026-11-14).

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"Pipeline stages: from raw FIRMS data to the harmonized series" ]

Stage 1 · Ingestion

The original FIRMS CSV files (MODIS, S-NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21) are read without copying them, and only what falls inside the region's bounding rectangle is kept: of 146.3 million rows read, 8.04 million remain. If there are days that FIRMS does publish but that are missing locally, only those gaps are requested from its API. A cache avoids rereading files that have not changed, so a new run takes about 30 seconds.

Stage 2 · Standardization

Each detection goes through 10 rules, always in the same order, and everything that is discarded is stored together with the reason. For example:

Outside the country's real polygon: 694,486 detections.

Duplicates across files: 267,103.

Non-vegetation (volcanoes, industry, offshore): 211,100.

Fixed sources (gas flares, refineries, industry): 109,635.

6.86 million detections remain, each with its confidence (low, nominal or high), its H3 cell, its local solar day and the constellation of satellites active that day.

Stage 3 · Deduplication

The same fire can be seen several times in one day: by the five satellites, by day and by night. All those detections are grouped by H3 cell (about 5 km²) and day into a single event, which keeps the maximum fire radiative power (FRP), which satellites saw it and its confidence. The result is 2.67 million events. Those with nominal or high confidence feed the series, and low-confidence ones are kept for alerts.

Stage 4 · Calibration

This is the step that makes the whole period comparable. In Argentina there are 6 epochs depending on which satellites were active (from Terra alone up to the full 5-satellite constellation).

-Ratio between epochs: in each epoch, the previous one is simulated by removing satellites, and we measure how many more events the larger constellation sees over the same fires. This is done by month of the year, because the gain changes with the season.

-Smoothing and chaining: the 12 ratios are smoothed with a circular harmonic fit and multiplied up to the reference constellation, which yields a K factor per epoch and month.

-Uncertainty and validation: each factor carries a 95% confidence interval (bootstrap). In validation, the monthly error for the pre-2012 epoch dropped from 27.7% to 10.1% compared with a single factor.

The harmonized series for each day is observed events × K[constellation of the day][month].

Stage 4b · Web data store

The results are packaged in a self-contained folder that the web app consumes without running the pipeline: events in Parquet partitioned by layer (SP, final, or NRT, provisional) and year, daily and monthly series with confidence intervals, K factors and a manifest with the sha256 of every file. Each record carries its harmonized weight and the calibration version it was computed with, and publication is atomic: the web app never reads a half-written store.

Stage 4c · Quality audit

An independent script, which imports nothing from the pipeline, tries to break the results before they are declared final. It checks schema and nulls, location and duplicates, artificial jumps at every constellation change, and consistency of totals. In the Argentina run it found and fixed 9 problems, including satellite outages treated as "no fire", gas flares inflating cells, and an artificial +43% jump at Aqua's entry that dropped to +14%. The final status is 19 PASS, 26 WARN (mostly by-design behaviors) and 0 FAIL, and the audit acts as a publication gate: with any FAIL, nothing is published.

Engineering built to scale

Partitioned Parquet data, to read only what is needed for the queried area.

Streaming processing with less than 300 MB of RAM, so it does not require expensive infrastructure.

Validated in Argentina and designed to extend to more than 150 countries without changing the architecture.

Next stages toward the web application

The historical pipeline, the web data store and the audit are already implemented for Argentina. What comes next:

-Stage 5 · Validation and robustness: compare against burned-area products (BA_MODIS and BA_VIIRS), run sensitivity tests, and run another country, such as Chile or Brazil, without touching the code.

-Stage 6 · Analytical products: climatology and anomalies against a baseline period, trends (Mann-Kendall and Sen's slope) and aggregation by province and department.

-Stage 7 · Real time and alerts: periodic polling of NOAA-21 near real time and an alert for any new detection, prioritized by confidence, FRP and proximity to sensitive areas. FIRMS publishes about 3 hours after the satellite pass, which is a limitation of the source.

-Stage 8 · Global scaling: two layers (consolidated historical and recent) and calibration by latitude zones and hemisphere, so that any query is answered by reading and summing weights.

-Stages 9 to 11 · API, web application and operations: a backend with series, events, anomalies and alerts; an interactive map with H3 hexagons and an alerts panel; and deployment with monitoring and versioning.

3. What is the impact?

Today, fire managers do not have a consistent picture of when and where burning occurred, because the record is fragmented across sensors. Virtual Satellite Unification removes that fragmentation and enables decisions based on a complete 26-year history.

Anticipate critical periods: identifying in which months and zones activity tends to concentrate makes it possible to prepare resources before the season starts.

Guide monitoring: direct surveillance and sensors toward the areas and dates where they are needed most.

Improve response: having a reference for what is normal makes it possible to quickly recognize an anomalous season and escalate the alert in time.

Better science: long, homogeneous series make it possible to study trends, unusual conditions and the relationship between fire, climate and land use without instrument artifacts.

Access for everyone: any organization, from an emergency service to a research team, can use it from the browser without technical knowledge of remote sensing.

4. What sets it apart from the rest?

A single virtual satellite instead of five sources: the user does not need to know which sensor detected what; they see one single series.

Explicit, reproducible harmonization: calibration by constellation and month (K factor) is a clear method, not a stack of layers.

Location-agnostic: it is not tied to one country or ecosystem; the same pipeline works for any region.

Lightweight: it runs on less than 300 MB of RAM thanks to streaming and the Parquet format.

Decision-oriented: it does not just show points on a map, it tells you what is normal and what is anomalous.

5. What are the benefits of using it?

Time savings: weeks of manual cleaning, deduplication and calibration of data from different sensors are eliminated.

Confidence in comparison: an increase in the series reflects more fire, not a change of instrument.

Instant historical perspective: more than two decades of context for any chosen area of interest.

Alerts with a rationale: the anomaly provides an objective threshold for declaring a season out of the ordinary.

Open, reusable data: the CSV download makes it possible to integrate the results into your own reports, dashboards or systems.

Low operating cost: its memory efficiency makes it viable for organizations with few resources to use it.

Easy to grow: adding new countries or new satellites does not require redesigning the solution.

Data source: NASA FIRMS (Fire Information for Resource Management System) – MODIS, VIIRS S-NPP, VIIRS NOAA-20 and VIIRS NOAA-21.
